display.text:
# Telemetry

celld can record traces and logs for the requests it serves. The
feature is off by default, and the off state costs nothing. Set
`CELLD_OTEL=1` to turn it on.

The default sink is the fleet bucket. celld writes Parquet files under
the `telemetry/` prefix, so a fleet with a bucket has observability
with no other service. DuckDB can query these files directly. An
alternative sink sends the same data to an OpenTelemetry collector.

The schema is version `v0-unstable`. The column names can change
before a stable release, and each file carries the schema version in
its object metadata.

## Configuration

| variable | default | effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CELLD_OTEL` | `0` | Set this value to `1` to enable telemetry. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_SINK` | `bucket` | `bucket` writes Parquet to the fleet bucket. `otlp` sends OTLP/HTTP protobuf to a collector instead. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_BUCKET` | the fleet bucket | A different bucket for the Parquet files, on the same endpoint and credentials. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_RETENTION` | `30d` | celld deletes telemetry files older than this. `none` disables the deletion, so your own lifecycle rules can control the data. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS` | `300000` | celld writes a Parquet file after this many milliseconds of buffered events. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES` | `5242880` | celld writes a Parquet file after the buffered events reach this many bytes. celld uses the limit it reaches first. |
| `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` | `parentbased_always_on` | A standard sampler name. `traceidratio` with `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` records a fraction of the traces. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | `http://localhost:4318` | The collector base URL, for the `otlp` sink. `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` also apply. |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `celld` | The service name in the exported resource. |

The `bucket` sink requires the node to have a fleet bucket
(`CELLD_BUCKET`). The `otlp` sink works on a node without one.

## What celld records

celld records a span for each request a stateless Worker serves, for
each event a cell serves (a fetch, an alarm, an RPC, a WebSocket
message), for each outbound `fetch()`, and for each cell start. A
span carries the request id, the cell, the isolate, the
queue wait, the outbound URL and status, and the durability facts the
runtime already knows.

celld also records each `console.log` line as a log record. The log
record carries the trace id and the span id of the handler that wrote
it, so a query can join the logs to the traces. The correlation
survives `await`.

celld reads the W3C `traceparent` header on incoming requests, so its
spans join the trace of the system in front of it. celld sends a
`traceparent` header on outbound `fetch()`, so downstream systems can
join too. A Worker call to a Durable Object stays in one trace.

The sampler decides at the start of a request. An unsampled request
records nothing and costs almost nothing. Under load, telemetry sheds
before requests do, and celld counts what it sheds.

celld records no metrics yet. The spans carry the durations and the
queue waits, so many questions a metric answers have an answer in the
traces, and a metrics signal can come later without a change to the
trace schema.

## Query the bucket with DuckDB

```sql
INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;
CREATE SECRET celld_telemetry (
  TYPE s3, KEY_ID '...', SECRET '...',
  ENDPOINT 's3.example.com', URL_STYLE 'path'
);
CREATE VIEW traces AS SELECT * FROM
  read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/*/*/*/*/*/*.parquet');
CREATE VIEW logs AS SELECT * FROM
  read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/logs/*/*/*/*/*/*.parquet');

-- The slowest requests.
SELECT name, duration_us, trace_id FROM traces
  ORDER BY duration_us DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Every log line, inside the span that wrote it.
SELECT l.body, t.name, t.duration_us FROM logs l
  JOIN traces t ON l.trace_id = t.trace_id AND l.span_id = t.span_id;
```

An S3-compatible endpoint such as minio needs `URL_STYLE 'path'` in
the secret, and a plain-HTTP endpoint also needs `USE_SSL false`. AWS
itself does not need either.

The files are partitioned by node and by hour:
`telemetry/traces/<node>/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/<hh>/<id>.parquet`. A query
that reads one day therefore touches only that day's files.

## File size and compaction

celld writes one Parquet file for each flush, on a time limit or a
size limit, whichever it reaches first. The defaults are 5 minutes
(`CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS=300000`) and 5 MB (`CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES=5242880`).

Keep the defaults if you run no compaction job. They make files large
enough for a fast query with no other moving part. A query sees an
event up to 5 minutes after the request, so the default suits an
investigation after the fact.

Set `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS=10000` for a near-live view, such as a
dashboard or an active debug session: a query then sees an event
within 10 seconds. A short flush makes many small files, and DuckDB
opens every file a query reads, so you must also run the compaction
job below. Turn on the compaction job first, then shorten the flush,
or queries grow slow within hours.

The `otlp` sink is the other route to a near-live view. It sends each
batch to a collector, so set the same short `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS`.

## Compaction

Run a compaction job on a maintenance node, not on a celld node. celld
does not compact its own files, because the serving path must not do
storage maintenance and each node writes only the files it produced.

The job rewrites one past hour of small files into one large file.
DuckDB does the work:

```sql
COPY (
  SELECT * FROM
    read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/<node>/2026/08/09/22/*.parquet')
  ORDER BY start_unix_us
) TO 's3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/<node>/2026/08/09/22/compacted.parquet'
  (FORMAT parquet, COMPRESSION zstd);
```

Run the job once an hour, for the hour that just ended. Do not compact
the current hour, because a node still writes to it. Delete the source
files after DuckDB writes the compacted file. The compacted file is
also smaller, because zstd compresses one sorted batch better than
many separate files.

1: # Testing
2: 
3: celld makes three important promises:
4: 
5: - An acknowledged write is durable.
6: - A cell has one writer at a time. It never has two.
7: - Code written for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects operates the
8:   same on celld.
9: 
10: We try to break each promise at the layer where a failure shows most
11: clearly. We test the API contract with differential execution against the
12: Cloudflare runtime. We check the coordination protocol against an
13: exhaustively model-checked specification, and we test it with
14: deterministic simulation. We test the full system with fault injection
15: on live fleets.
16: 
17: ## Conformance: two runtimes, one output
18: 
19: We test the compatibility promise differentially. We run each Workers and
20: Durable Objects program twice: once on workerd, the runtime binary that
21: Cloudflare operates in production, and once on celld, on identical bytes.
22: The two outputs must be equal. This shows two facts at once: the program
23: is real Cloudflare code, because workerd accepts it, and celld obeys the
24: contract, because the outputs are equal. A test cannot agree with our own
25: runtime by accident.
26: 
27: The corpus only grows. When celld gets a new API surface, we add fixtures
28: for that surface, and the fixtures must give equal output on the two
29: engines. We also port test suites from workerd itself: the Durable
30: Objects contract, the web-platform globals, and the upstream Web Platform
31: Tests. Before a release, we also replay scenarios through the full
32: `celld` binary in each deployment mode: storage, SQL, alarms, streams,
33: WebSockets, and lifecycle.
34: 
35: ## Specification: exhaustive at small size
36: 
37: The coordination protocol is also specified in TLA+. Heyang Zhou wrote
38: the specifications against celld v0.1.0, and his model checking found
39: four bugs and a split-brain that lost an acknowledged write. All are
40: fixed. None had surfaced in our own review or testing.
41: 
42: Where simulation samples schedules, the checker enumerates them: at a
43: small configuration it visits every reachable state. The model grants
44: the implementation a linearizable object store and perfect shared
45: clocks, so a violation it finds needs no clock skew and no storage
46: anomaly to occur. The invariants are the first two promises at the top
47: of this page: one writer for each epoch, and no acknowledged write
48: lost. The fencing argument itself — that a stale owner's late writes
49: cannot cost an acknowledged write, because the epoch in the key keeps
50: its lineage apart — is checked, not asserted.
51: 
52: Every configuration carries a pinned expected verdict, and most of the
53: verdicts are failures: each failing configuration models a bug the
54: protocol once had, or a deliberately broken checker, and the model
55: must produce the counterexample. A configuration that stops failing
56: has lost its tooth. One tooth had already fallen out when the
57: specifications arrived; we repaired it.
58: 
59: Some specifications model a proposed protocol before it is built. When
60: the fence on write acknowledgments was redesigned, the design-stage
61: check produced an eight-state counterexample against the version it
62: replaced: a dormant cell resumes at its old epoch while its release is
63: in flight, acknowledges a write, and the takeover that follows
64: restores without it. The fix shipped; the counterexample stays as a
65: pinned failure.
66: 
67: The checker has also removed code: celld once sealed a cell's durable
68: history at restore, and the verdicts showed the seal defended only the
69: return of a write that was never acknowledged — an outcome celld does
70: not promise to prevent — while its permanent cut could turn a
71: recoverable ordering slip into a permanent loss. The seal is gone.
72: 
73: The specifications are a hand-synced snapshot, deliberately not in
74: continuous integration: a silently stale gate is worse than none. In
75: practice their updates have landed in the same changes that moved the
76: protocol, and a delta ledger records what the model does not yet
77: describe, including places where the model is weaker than the code
78: rather than wrong. Simulation remains the per-commit ratchet; the
79: model is its exhaustive small-configuration complement.
80: 
81: ## Simulation: the protocol under adversarial schedules
82: 
83: The dangerous bugs live in the coordination: a crash during an ownership
84: handoff, a lease renewal that races a takeover, an alarm that fires
85: against a partially restored cell. These windows are nanoseconds wide and
86: open rarely, so a test cannot wait for them.
87: 
88: Thus the coordination protocol is a
89: [pure decision core](https://github.com/denoland/celld/tree/main/crates/logic)
90: with no I/O of its own: the clock, the randomness, and the object store
91: are interfaces, and a simulator drives the core. The simulated store
92: injects latency, compare-and-swap races, and lost responses; the clocks
93: drift apart; a node can crash at each await point. Scripted adversaries
94: play the cells: a handler that never returns, a write stream that stops
95: halfway. V8 stays out of the simulation, because V8 is not deterministic.
96: 
97: A seeded scheduler drives each run, so a failure is not a fluke: the seed
98: replays it exactly, every time, and we keep the seed until the bug is
99: dead. We examine each property for safety (two writers in one epoch, a
100: lost acknowledged write, an expired lease that comes back) and for
101: liveness (each armed alarm fires, and ownership settles on one node after
102: a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
103: core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.
104: 
105: Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
106: we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
107: protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
108: A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.
109: 
110: ## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see
111: 
112: Simulation cannot see the real S3 tail latency, the real kernel and
113: filesystem behavior, or V8 under memory pressure. The third layer is
114: therefore a permanent fleet lab: standard VMs from standard providers,
115: and a real bucket. The workloads rotate: chat rooms under many WebSocket
116: connections, working sets that shift across tens of thousands of cells
117: (each cell has a unique checksum), deployment cutovers under load, and
118: runs that fill the nodes to the memory limit. The lab qualifies each
119: release, and between releases it pushes the density and the fault
120: coverage further. Each run makes an archived evidence bundle: the
121: configuration, the verification sweeps, the node journals, the kernel
122: logs, and the phase timings. We keep a red run with the same care as a
123: green run, because a failure that the harness caught is a result, not a
124: retry.
125: 
126: We inject the faults between verification passes. A pass fetches each
127: cell through different nodes and compares the durable state exactly: the
128: status, the body, and the full message ledger. Each run therefore has a
129: clean picture before the fault and after it. A cell can be unavailable
130: for a short time while its ownership moves, but its committed state must
131: stay complete, and a live node must serve that state again.
132: 
133: The scenarios attack every seam that we know:
134: 
135: - Stop a node with `SIGKILL` in the middle of a write stream and delete
136:   its local database, so recovery can only come from the bucket. Every
137:   acknowledged write comes back, because the output gate held each
138:   response until the write was durable.
139: - Freeze an owner node, write to its cells through other nodes, and
140:   unfreeze it. The node sees that its lease moved and refuses to serve
141:   the old state, and each write from the other nodes lands exactly one
142:   time: one epoch has at most one writer.
143: - Cut a node off from the bucket. It fences itself, because a node that
144:   cannot replicate must not own cells.
145: - Throttle the bucket, so it answers each request with a 429. The engine
146:   slows to the write rate of the store and does not amplify the
147:   throttle, because a node that knows its replicated position does not
148:   ask a slow store for extra listings.
149: - Stop a full host at the provider level in the middle of a workload.
150:   Its cells move to the other nodes, and the returning host joins again
151:   with no duplicate residency.
152: 
153: Across every run of every scenario, no acknowledged write was lost and
154: no committed state was damaged; the verification sweeps show zero body
155: faults, zero status faults, and zero lost messages.
156: 
157: ## A few numbers we trust
158: 
159: Each number includes the condition of its measurement. A number without
160: its conditions has no value.
161: 
162: - **The epoch fence holds under contention.** Five hundred claimants
163:   tried at the same time to own the same cells: 5,500 attempts, one
164:   writer for each epoch, zero violations.
165: - **A warm resident request is local.** A request to a resident cell does
166:   zero bucket operations and returns in p50 ~1.1 ms and p99 ~7 ms (a
167:   fixed-host measurement). Only a cold activation touches object storage.
168: - **A durable write waits for a durability proof.** A single node proves
169:   each write through the bucket, so one storage round trip is the minimum
170:   latency for that write. A fleet of two or more nodes can prove a write
171:   when each follower holds it on disk, and a follower fsync is much
172:   faster than a storage round trip: a lab fleet measured about 600 ms for
173:   a bucket proof and about 25 ms for a fleet proof. The bucket upload
174:   races every fleet proof and either one proves the write, so a slow
175:   follower cannot make a write slower than a bucket proof. Concurrent
176:   writes to one cell join one shared upload, so the throughput of one
177:   cell is not one round trip for each write.
178: - **A restore is normal work.** Placement handles the restore of an
179:   inactive cell as ordinary work, and not as an emergency procedure. The
180:   measured restore times come from the retired external replicator, so this
181:   page gives no number until a fleet run measures `celld-ltx`.
182: - **Ten small nodes held real scale.** A fleet of ten nodes, each with 4
183:   vCPU and 8 GB, held 10,000 resident cells and 20,000 concurrent
184:   WebSocket connections. We stopped two of the ten nodes, and the data of
185:   every cell was available again on another node in ~11 s at the tail
186:   (with reserve headroom).
187: 
188: ## The failure edges we intend to find
189: 
190: We must also know where a policy stops, so we record the edges instead of
191: tuning them away. The clearest edge is the reserve headroom: a fleet that
192: is full to its resident limit has no space for the cells of a lost node,
193: so a failure of more than one node at the limit degrades the service,
194: and a fleet with headroom does not. We measure both sides of that line,
195: the good restoration with reserve and the red case without, because this
196: measurement is part of the work.
197: 
198: If you find an edge that we did not find, tell us: a schedule that breaks
199: a promise, a fault that we did not inject, a number that you cannot
200: reproduce. That is exactly the bug report that we want:
201: [github.com/denoland/celld/issues](https://github.com/denoland/celld/issues).

(End of file - total 201 lines)

dead. We examine each property for safety (two writers in one epoch, a
lost acknowledged write, an expired lease that comes back) and for
liveness (each armed alarm fires, and ownership settles on one node after
a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.

Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.

## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see

Simulation cannot see the real S3 tail latency, the real kernel and
filesystem behavior, or V8 under memory pressure. The third layer is
therefore a permanent fleet lab: standard VMs from standard providers,
and a real bucket. The workloads rotate: chat rooms under many WebSocket
connections, working sets that shift across tens of thousands of cells
(each cell has a unique checksum), deployment cutovers under load, and
runs that fill the nodes to the memory limit. The lab qualifies each
release, and between releases it pushes the density and the fault
coverage further. Each run makes an archived evidence bundle: the
configuration, the verification sweeps, the node journals, the kernel
logs, and the phase timings. We keep a red run with the same care as a
green run, because a failure that the harness caught is a result, not a
retry.

We inject the faults between verification passes. A pass fetches each
cell through different nodes and compares the durable state exactly: the
status, the body, and the full message ledger. Each run therefore has a
clean picture before the fault and after it. A cell can be unavailable
for a short time while its ownership moves, but its committed state must
stay complete, and a live node must serve that state again.

The scenarios attack every seam that we know:

- Stop a node with `SIGKILL` in the middle of a write stream and delete
  its local database, so recovery can only come from the bucket. Every
  acknowledged write comes back, because the output gate held each
  response until the write was durable.
- Freeze an owner node, write to its cells through other nodes, and
  unfreeze it. The node sees that its lease moved and refuses to serve
  the old state, and each write from the other nodes lands exactly one
  time: one epoch has at most one writer.
- Cut a node off from the bucket. It fences itself, because a node that
  cannot replicate must not own cells.
- Throttle the bucket, so it answers each request with a 429. The engine
  slows to the write rate of the store and does not amplify the
  throttle, because a node that knows its replicated position does not
  ask a slow store for extra listings.
- Stop a full host at the provider level in the middle of a workload.
  Its cells move to the other nodes, and the returning host joins again
  with no duplicate residency.

Across every run of every scenario, no acknowledged write was lost and
no committed state was damaged; the verification sweeps show zero body
faults, zero status faults, and zero lost messages.

## A few numbers we trust

Each number includes the condition of its measurement. A number without
its conditions has no value.

- **The epoch fence holds under contention.** Five hundred claimants
  tried at the same time to own the same cells: 5,500 attempts, one
  writer for each epoch, zero violations.
- **A warm resident request is local.** A request to a resident cell does
  zero bucket operations and returns in p50 ~1.1 ms and p99 ~7 ms (a
  fixed-host measurement). Only a cold activation touches object storage.
- **A durable write waits for a durability proof.** A single node proves
  each write through the bucket, so one storage round trip is the minimum
  latency for that write. A fleet of two or more nodes can prove a write
  when each follower holds it on disk, and a follower fsync is much
  faster than a storage round trip: a lab fleet measured about 600 ms for
  a bucket proof and about 25 ms for a fleet proof. The bucket upload
  races every fleet proof and either one proves the write, so a slow
  follower cannot make a write slower than a bucket proof. Concurrent
  writes to one cell join one shared upload, so the throughput of one
  cell is not one round trip for each write.
- **A restore is normal work.** Placement handles the restore of an
  inactive cell as ordinary work, and not as an emergency procedure. The
  measured restore times come from the retired external replicator, so this
  page gives no number until a fleet run measures `celld-ltx`.
- **Ten small nodes held real scale.** A fleet of ten nodes, each with 4
  vCPU and 8 GB, held 10,000 resident cells and 20,000 concurrent
  WebSocket connections. We stopped two of the ten nodes, and the data of
  every cell was available again on another node in ~11 s at the tail
  (with reserve headroom).

## The failure edges we intend to find

We must also know where a policy stops, so we record the edges instead of
tuning them away. The clearest edge is the reserve headroom: a fleet that
is full to its resident limit has no space for the cells of a lost node,
so a failure of more than one node at the limit degrades the service,
and a fleet with headroom does not. We measure both sides of that line,
the good restoration with reserve and the red case without, because this
measurement is part of the work.

If you find an edge that we did not find, tell us: a schedule that breaks
a promise, a fault that we did not inject, a number that you cannot
reproduce. That is exactly the bug report that we want:
[github.com/denoland/celld/issues](https://github.com/denoland/celld/issues).

27: | [Workflows](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/workers-api/) | **Partial** |
28: | [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/workers/workers-api-reference/) | **Partial** |

31: | [Hyperdrive](https://developers.cloudflare.com/hyperdrive/) | **No** |
32: | [Browser Rendering](https://developers.cloudflare.com/browser-rendering/) | **No** |
33: | [Email Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-routing/email-workers/) | **No** |
34: | [Python Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/languages/python/) | **No** |
35: 
36: ### [Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/)
37: 
38: **Partial**
39: 
40: - The [runtime API table](#runtime-apis) lists the Worker runtime gaps.
41: - celld does not manage a custom domain or terminate TLS. Terminate TLS in the
42:   ingress proxy.
43: - An experimental Workers AI HTTP adapter is available through
44:   `CELLD_AI_URL`.
45: 
46: ### [Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/)
47: 
48: **Partial**
49: 
50: - An RPC stub cannot cross an isolate boundary. See [RPC](#rpc).
51: - An outbound WebSocket does not continue after the object moves to another
52:   node.
53: - celld refuses invalid UTF-8 from a SQLite `TEXT` value. Store arbitrary
54:   bytes in a `BLOB`.
55: - `SqlStorage.Cursor.toArray()` gives a celld-specific error when the isolate
56:   is near its V8 heap limit.
57: 
58: ### [Cron Triggers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/)
59: 
60: **Partial**
61: 
62: - celld rejects a descending range such as `SAT-SUN` or `NOV-FEB`.
63: - celld rejects `*` inside a list such as `1,*`.
64: - celld runs one handler for each occurrence across the complete fleet.
65: - After fleet downtime, celld runs the most recent missed occurrence one time.
66: - celld runs one handler at a time for each script. It retries a failed handler
67:   until the next occurrence unless the handler calls `noRetry()`.
68: - A service-binding target cannot run its own Cron Triggers.
69: 
70: ### [Worker Loader](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/worker-loader/)
71: 
72: **Partial**
73: 
74: - Worker Loader is experimental and requires `CELLD_WORKER_LOADER=LOADER`.
75: - A `globalOutbound` Fetcher is not available.
76: - A loaded Worker cannot receive a capability stub in `env`.
77: - Awaitable and pipelined properties are not available.
78: 
79: ### [KV](https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/api/)
80: 
81: **Partial**
82: 
83: - celld has no edge cache. `cacheTtl` has no effect, and `cacheStatus` is
84:   `null`.
85: - A value above 1 MiB requires a fleet bucket.
86: - celld stores a separate object when an application writes an identical large
87:   value after a namespace changes owners. The separate object prevents an old
88:   owner from deleting the current value.
89: - celld reads a large-value row from an older release, but it does not reclaim
90:   the legacy object after the row is removed.
91: - A namespace has one writer. Use more namespaces to increase write capacity.
92: - A namespace ID can use the Cloudflare hexadecimal form or another stable
93:   string.
94: 
95: ### [Queues](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/)
96: 
97: **Partial**
98: 
99: - A queue has one writer. Use more queues to increase write capacity.
100: - A Queue owner accepts two concurrent producer operations. One operation can
101:   run and one operation can wait, so an overload cannot delay Queue alarms.
102:   The owner refuses an additional operation, and the producer can retry it.
103: - A queue can have one consumer script. The consumer cannot also export a
104:   `fetch()` handler.
105: - celld retains a message for four days. You cannot configure this period.
106: - Pull consumers and the Queues HTTP API are not available.
107: - Dashboard controls, manual consumer attachment, R2 event notifications, and
108:   Queue event subscriptions are not available.
109: 
110: ### [D1](https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/worker-api/d1-database/)
111: 
112: **Partial**
113: 
114: - A binding result can contain at most 100,000 rows or 32 MiB.
115: - celld refuses invalid UTF-8 from a SQLite `TEXT` value. Store arbitrary
116:   bytes in a `BLOB`.
117: 
118: ### [Workflows](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/workers-api/)
119: 
120: **Partial**
121: 
122: - `create()` replaces a terminal instance that has the same ID. Cloudflare
123:   refuses each duplicate ID.
124: - celld replays `run()` from the start, so code outside a step runs again.
125: - A crash after a step side effect can run the step callback again.
126: - `retention` and `locationHint` are not available.
127: - Non-step work cannot remain pending for more than 60 seconds.
128: - A step result, an event payload, and the workflow parameters each have a
129:   1 MiB limit.
130: - `pause()` stops a queued or waiting instance immediately. It lets an active
131:   step finish, and the status changes from `waitingForPause` to `paused` before
132:   the next step starts.
133: - `resume()` starts a paused instance and cancels a pending pause. A paused
134:   retry, sleep, or event wait keeps its remaining wait duration.
135: - `restart()` starts a new generation from the beginning by default. Its
136:   `from` option can select a step by its `name`, `count`, and `type`. The
137:   `count` value defaults to `1`, and the `type` value defaults to `do`.
138: - A selected restart reuses each result before the selected step and reruns
139:   that step and each later step. The runtime rejects a selector that does not
140:   match the execution history.
141: - `delete()`, `deleteBatch()`, and rollback are not available.
142: - A sensitive step result and a `ReadableStream` step result are not
143:   available.
144: 
145: ### [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/workers/workers-api-reference/)
146: 
147: **Partial**
148: 
149: - An R2 binding uses the fleet bucket under `r2/<bucket_name>/`.
150: - `ssecKey` is not available.
151: - A conditional write cannot use a streamed body larger than 8 MiB.
152: - `createMultipartUpload()` does not accept a checksum.
153: - A multipart upload cannot resume on another node or after a restart.
154: - celld cannot replace a multipart part that the object store already holds.
155: - Out-of-order parts can use at most 256 MiB of memory, and completion cannot
156:   change the order of stored parts.
157: - `jurisdiction` is not available.
158: 
159: ## Runtime APIs
160: 
161: | API | status |
162: | --- | --- |
163: | [Fetch, Request, Response, and Headers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/fetch/) | **Partial** |
164: | [Bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/) | **Partial** |
165: | [Context](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/context/) | **Partial** |
166: | [Handlers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/handlers/) | **Partial** |
167: | [RPC](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/rpc/) | **Partial** |
168: | [Streams](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/streams/) | **Partial** |
169: | [Encoding](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/encoding/) | **Yes** |
170: | [WebSockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/websockets/) | **Partial** |
171: | [Web Crypto](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/web-crypto/) | **Partial** |
172: | [Web standards](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/web-standards/) | **Partial** |
173: | [WebAssembly](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/webassembly/) | **Yes** |
174: | [Performance and timers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/performance/) | **Partial** |
175: | [Console](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/console/) | **Partial** |
176: | [Node.js compatibility](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/nodejs/) | **Partial** |
177: | [Facets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dynamic-workers/usage/durable-object-facets/) | **No** |
178: | [Cache](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/cache/) | **No** |
179: | [HTMLRewriter](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/html-rewriter/) | **No** |
180: | [TCP sockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/tcp-sockets/) | **No** |
181: | [EventSource](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/eventsource/) | **No** |
182: | [MessageChannel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/messagechannel/) | **No** |
183: | BroadcastChannel | **No** |
184: 
185: ### [Fetch, Request, Response, and Headers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/fetch/)
186: 
187: **Partial**
188: 
189: - The `cache` request option is not available.
190: - celld removes `Content-Length` from a Worker response. It preserves the
191:   header for a `HEAD` response.
192: - A remote Durable Object call streams the request body to the owner. The call
193:   cannot retry after body transmission starts because celld keeps no replay
194:   copy.
195: 
196: ### [Bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/)
197: 
198: **Partial**
199: 
200: - The [services table](#services) lists the available binding types.
201: - celld supports Durable Objects, services, variables, assets, D1, KV, Queues,
202:   Workflows, and R2 bindings. Each other binding type is not available.
203: 
204: ### [Context](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/context/)
205: 
206: **Partial**
207: 
208: - `passThroughOnException()` has no effect because celld has no CDN fallback.
209: - `ctx.facets` is not defined.
210: 
211: ### [Handlers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/handlers/)
212: 
213: **Partial**
214: 
215: - The `tail` and `email` handlers are not available.
216: 
217: ### [RPC](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/rpc/)
218: 
219: **Partial**
220: 
221: - A cross-isolate named service binding supports only a single method call. It
222:   does not support `fetch()`, awaitable properties, or pipelined paths.
223: - An RPC stub cannot cross an isolate boundary.
224: - `ctx.exports` contains only the entrypoints that the configuration declares.
225: 
226: ### [Streams](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/streams/)
227: 
228: **Partial**
229: 
230: - `ReadableStream.from()` is not available.
231: 
232: ### [WebSockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/websockets/)
233: 
234: **Partial**
235: 
236: - `getTags()` is not available.
237: - A caller must call `accept()` on the socket from a subrequest upgrade.
238: - An outbound Worker socket closes after the response and `waitUntil` work
239:   end.
240: - celld rejects an upgrade when the response status is not 101.
241: - celld removes Worker-supplied protocol and connection headers from an upgrade
242:   response.
243: - An outbound upgrade combines repeated values for one header name.
244: - `acceptWebSocket()` throws when the isolate uses more than 90 percent of its
245:   V8 heap limit.
246: 
247: ### [Web Crypto](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/web-crypto/)
248: 
249: **Partial**
250: 
251: - `wrapKey()` and `unwrapKey()` are not available.
252: - RSA-PSS signing is not available.
253: - Web Crypto does not provide HKDF or PBKDF2 through `deriveBits()`. Use
254:   `node:crypto` for these algorithms.
255: 
256: ### [Web standards](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/web-standards/)
257: 
258: **Partial**
259: 
260: - An `AbortSignal` does not abort an RPC call.
261: - `signal.onabort` has no effect. Use `addEventListener("abort", ...)`.
262: - `structuredClone()` is not conformant for some exotic types.
263: 
264: ### [Performance and timers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/performance/)
265: 
266: **Partial**
267: 
268: - An active interval keeps a Worker request open.
269: - `performance.now()` has millisecond resolution.
270: - The other `performance` properties are stubs.
271: 
272: ### [Console](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/console/)
273: 
274: **Partial**
275: 
276: - `debug`, `trace`, `group`, and `table` have no effect.
277: - `assert`, `time`, and `count` are not available.
278: 
279: ### [Node.js compatibility](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/nodejs/)
280: 
281: **Partial**
282: 
283: - celld implements `node:assert`, `node:async_hooks`, `node:buffer`,
284:   `node:events`, `node:path`, `node:stream`, `node:timers/promises`, and
285:   `node:util`.
286: - `node:crypto` does not implement Diffie-Hellman, streaming signatures,
287:   ciphers, RSA-PSS, or DSA signatures and key generation.
288: - `node:zlib` implements only the synchronous gzip and deflate functions.
289: - `node:fs` returns `ENOENT` from each read.
290: - Each other Node.js module returns an inert stub. This behavior is a known
291:   silent gap.
292: 
293: ### [TCP sockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/tcp-sockets/)
294: 
295: **No**
296: 
297: - `connect()` returns an inert stub. This behavior is a known silent gap.
298: 
299: ### EventSource, MessageChannel, and BroadcastChannel
300: 
301: **No**
302: 
303: - These classes are inert stubs. This behavior is a known silent gap.
304: 
305: ## Compatibility flags
306: 
307: celld honors these compatibility switches:
308: 
309: - `delete_all_deletes_alarm`
310: - `js_rpc`
311: - `fetcher_no_get_put_delete`
312: - `sqlite_vec`
313: - `websocket_standard_binary_type`
314: - The static-assets navigation flags
315: 
316: celld accepts each other compatibility flag without effect.
317: `Cloudflare.compatibilityFlags` reports only the flags that celld honors.
318: 
319: ## Wrangler configuration
320: 
321: `celld deploy` accepts `wrangler.jsonc` or `wrangler.json`. It does not
322: accept `wrangler.toml`. The deployment accepts these top-level keys:
323: 
324: - `$schema`, `name`, `main`, and `no_bundle`
325: - `compatibility_date` and `compatibility_flags`
326: - `durable_objects` and `migrations`
327: - `assets`, `services`, `triggers`, and `vars`
328: - `d1_databases`, `kv_namespaces`, `queues`, `workflows`, and
329:   `r2_buckets`
330: 
331: Each other top-level key, including `routes`, stops the deployment.
332: An asset-only project can omit `main`. celld refuses a symlink or special file
333: in an asset directory, and `.assetsignore` requires Wrangler.
334: 
335: See [Limitations](limitations.md) for the operating-system, networking,
336: security, pressure, and update boundaries.

(End of file - total 336 lines)
</content>

- Awaitable and pipelined properties are not available.

### [KV](https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/api/)

**Partial**

- celld has no edge cache. `cacheTtl` has no effect, and `cacheStatus` is
  `null`.
- A value above 1 MiB requires a fleet bucket.
- celld stores a separate object when an application writes an identical large
  value after a namespace changes owners. The separate object prevents an old
  owner from deleting the current value.
- celld reads a large-value row from an older release, but it does not reclaim
  the legacy object after the row is removed.
- A namespace has one writer. Use more namespaces to increase write capacity.
- A namespace ID can use the Cloudflare hexadecimal form or another stable
  string.

### [Queues](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/)

**Partial**

- A queue has one writer. Use more queues to increase write capacity.
- A Queue owner accepts two concurrent producer operations. One operation can
  run and one operation can wait, so an overload cannot delay Queue alarms.
  The owner refuses an additional operation, and the producer can retry it.
- A queue can have one consumer script. The consumer cannot also export a
  `fetch()` handler.
- celld retains a message for four days. You cannot configure this period.
- Pull consumers and the Queues HTTP API are not available.
- Dashboard controls, manual consumer attachment, R2 event notifications, and
  Queue event subscriptions are not available.

### [D1](https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/worker-api/d1-database/)

**Partial**

- A binding result can contain at most 100,000 rows or 32 MiB.
- celld refuses invalid UTF-8 from a SQLite `TEXT` value. Store arbitrary
  bytes in a `BLOB`.

### [Workflows](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/workers-api/)

**Partial**

- `create()` replaces a terminal instance that has the same ID. Cloudflare
  refuses each duplicate ID.
- celld replays `run()` from the start, so code outside a step runs again.
- A crash after a step side effect can run the step callback again.
- `retention` and `locationHint` are not available.
- Non-step work cannot remain pending for more than 60 seconds.
- A step result, an event payload, and the workflow parameters each have a
  1 MiB limit.
- `pause()` stops a queued or waiting instance immediately. It lets an active
  step finish, and the status changes from `waitingForPause` to `paused` before
  the next step starts.
- `resume()` starts a paused instance and cancels a pending pause. A paused
  retry, sleep, or event wait keeps its remaining wait duration.
- `restart()` starts a new generation from the beginning by default. Its
  `from` option can select a step by its `name`, `count`, and `type`. The
  `count` value defaults to `1`, and the `type` value defaults to `do`.
- A selected restart reuses each result before the selected step and reruns
  that step and each later step. The runtime rejects a selector that does not
  match the execution history.
- `delete()`, `deleteBatch()`, and rollback are not available.
- A sensitive step result and a `ReadableStream` step result are not
  available.

### [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/workers/workers-api-reference/)

**Partial**

- An R2 binding uses the fleet bucket under `r2/<bucket_name>/`.
- `ssecKey` is not available.
- A conditional write cannot use a streamed body larger than 8 MiB.
- `createMultipartUpload()` does not accept a checksum.
- A multipart upload cannot resume on another node or after a restart.
- celld cannot replace a multipart part that the object store already holds.
- Out-of-order parts can use at most 256 MiB of memory, and completion cannot
  change the order of stored parts.
- `jurisdiction` is not available.

## Runtime APIs

| API | status |
| --- | --- |
| [Fetch, Request, Response, and Headers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/fetch/) | **Partial** |
| [Bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/) | **Partial** |
| [Context](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/context/) | **Partial** |
| [Handlers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/handlers/) | **Partial** |
| [RPC](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/rpc/) | **Partial** |
| [Streams](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/streams/) | **Partial** |
| [Encoding](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/encoding/) | **Yes** |
| [WebSockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/websockets/) | **Partial** |
| [Web Crypto](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/web-crypto/) | **Partial** |
| [Web standards](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/web-standards/) | **Partial** |
| [WebAssembly](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/webassembly/) | **Yes** |
| [Performance and timers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/performance/) | **Partial** |
| [Console](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/console/) | **Partial** |
| [Node.js compatibility](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/nodejs/) | **Partial** |
| [Facets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dynamic-workers/usage/durable-object-facets/) | **No** |
| [Cache](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/cache/) | **No** |
| [HTMLRewriter](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/html-rewriter/) | **No** |
| [TCP sockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/tcp-sockets/) | **No** |
| [EventSource](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/eventsource/) | **No** |
| [MessageChannel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/messagechannel/) | **No** |
| BroadcastChannel | **No** |

### [Fetch, Request, Response, and Headers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/fetch/)

**Partial**

- The `cache` request option is not available.
- celld removes `Content-Length` from a Worker response. It preserves the
  header for a `HEAD` response.
- A remote Durable Object call streams the request body to the owner. The call
  cannot retry after body transmission starts because celld keeps no replay
  copy.

### [Bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/)

**Partial**

- The [services table](#services) lists the available binding types.
- celld supports Durable Objects, services, variables, assets, D1, KV, Queues,
  Workflows, and R2 bindings. Each other binding type is not available.

### [Context](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/context/)

**Partial**

- `passThroughOnException()` has no effect because celld has no CDN fallback.
- `ctx.facets` is not defined.

### [Handlers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/handlers/)

**Partial**

- The `tail` and `email` handlers are not available.

### [RPC](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/rpc/)

**Partial**

- A cross-isolate named service binding supports only a single method call. It
  does not support `fetch()`, awaitable properties, or pipelined paths.
- An RPC stub cannot cross an isolate boundary.
- `ctx.exports` contains only the entrypoints that the configuration declares.

### [Streams](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/streams/)

**Partial**

- `ReadableStream.from()` is not available.

### [WebSockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/websockets/)

**Partial**

- `getTags()` is not available.
- A caller must call `accept()` on the socket from a subrequest upgrade.
- An outbound Worker socket closes after the response and `waitUntil` work
  end.
- celld rejects an upgrade when the response status is not 101.
- celld removes Worker-supplied protocol and connection headers from an upgrade
  response.
- An outbound upgrade combines repeated values for one header name.
- `acceptWebSocket()` throws when the isolate uses more than 90 percent of its
  V8 heap limit.

### [Web Crypto](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/web-crypto/)

**Partial**

- `wrapKey()` and `unwrapKey()` are not available.
- RSA-PSS signing is not available.
- Web Crypto does not provide HKDF or PBKDF2 through `deriveBits()`. Use
  `node:crypto` for these algorithms.

### [Web standards](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/web-standards/)

**Partial**

- An `AbortSignal` does not abort an RPC call.
- `signal.onabort` has no effect. Use `addEventListener("abort", ...)`.
- `structuredClone()` is not conformant for some exotic types.

### [Performance and timers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/performance/)

**Partial**

- An active interval keeps a Worker request open.
- `performance.now()` has millisecond resolution.
- The other `performance` properties are stubs.

### [Console](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/console/)

**Partial**

- `debug`, `trace`, `group`, and `table` have no effect.
- `assert`, `time`, and `count` are not available.

### [Node.js compatibility](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/nodejs/)

**Partial**

- celld implements `node:assert`, `node:async_hooks`, `node:buffer`,
  `node:events`, `node:path`, `node:stream`, `node:timers/promises`, and
  `node:util`.
- `node:crypto` does not implement Diffie-Hellman, streaming signatures,
  ciphers, RSA-PSS, or DSA signatures and key generation.
- `node:zlib` implements only the synchronous gzip and deflate functions.
- `node:fs` returns `ENOENT` from each read.
- Each other Node.js module returns an inert stub. This behavior is a known
  silent gap.

### [TCP sockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/tcp-sockets/)

**No**

- `connect()` returns an inert stub. This behavior is a known silent gap.

### EventSource, MessageChannel, and BroadcastChannel

**No**

- These classes are inert stubs. This behavior is a known silent gap.

## Compatibility flags

celld honors these compatibility switches:

- `delete_all_deletes_alarm`
- `js_rpc`
- `fetcher_no_get_put_delete`
- `sqlite_vec`
- `websocket_standard_binary_type`
- The static-assets navigation flags

celld accepts each other compatibility flag without effect.
`Cloudflare.compatibilityFlags` reports only the flags that celld honors.

## Wrangler configuration

`celld deploy` accepts `wrangler.jsonc` or `wrangler.json`. It does not
accept `wrangler.toml`. The deployment accepts these top-level keys:

- `$schema`, `name`, `main`, and `no_bundle`
- `compatibility_date` and `compatibility_flags`
- `durable_objects` and `migrations`
- `assets`, `services`, `triggers`, and `vars`
- `d1_databases`, `kv_namespaces`, `queues`, `workflows`, and
  `r2_buckets`

Each other top-level key, including `routes`, stops the deployment.
An asset-only project can omit `main`. celld refuses a symlink or special file
in an asset directory, and `.assetsignore` requires Wrangler.

See [Limitations](limitations.md) for the operating-system, networking,
security, pressure, and update boundaries.

display.text:
# Rust library API

## Select facade

Use `celld::asyncrt::select!` when the source order must not decide a tie. The
macro selects a cyclic start for each poll, and it rejects the `biased;` token.

Use `celld::asyncrt::select_biased!` only when the source order defines the
winner of a tie. The macro polls the branches in source order. The first token
must be a non-empty string literal that states which arm wins and why.

## Durability ownership

The `celld` crate requires one `node_log::DurabilityOwner` for each local
durability stack. The owner keeps the coupled registration. It retains each
live or failed background-task handle until shutdown joins it. It also retains
each admitted release-close task and the final close handle until the
registered managed databases close.

The crate removes these public functions:

- `LtxRepl::set_shipper`
- `LtxRepl::set_bundle_sink`
- `node_log::spawn_maintenance`
- `node_log::spawn_fragment_gc`

The old setter functions installed separate strong references. A
`NodeLogManager` also retains its `LtxRepl`, so these references can create an
ownership cycle.

The old spawn functions detached their task handles. An embedding process
therefore cannot stop or join the tasks during local shutdown.

Construct a `DurabilityOwner` after the node-log recovery completes. Call
`DurabilityOwner::start_background` before the process starts its application
services, and retain the owner for the process lifetime.

Await `LtxRepl::release` when a runtime stops a cell and keeps its local files.
The method admits a managed database close to the owner task group before it
waits. Require an `Ok` result before another activation reuses the local path.
The owner retains the admitted close if the caller is cancelled. An `Err`
result retains the replica, so a later call can retry while the owner accepts
close work. The final owner shutdown also closes a retained replica.

Call `DurabilityOwner::quiesce_and_seal_within` with the remaining process time
during shutdown. A `false` result means that the local fallback ran. Therefore,
the process must not prepare a clean reload.

Stop and join all application and runtime operations before the final local
shutdown. This order prevents an activation from retaining an unregistered
database across the final shutdown snapshot.

Call `DurabilityOwner::shutdown_local_within` after an optional clean-reload
preparation. Pass the remaining process time to this method. A `false` result
means that the local fallback ran before the local shutdown completed, so the
process must exit without unwinding.

A process that has a follower store without a runtime durability stack must
use `DurabilityOwner::new_follower`. This owner starts, stops, and joins the
follower fragment collector.

# Limitations

celld is an alpha. The current release has these operational limits. See
[Cloudflare compatibility](cloudflare-compat.md) for the supported services,
APIs, and Wrangler configuration.

## Fleets

- A fleet runs one application. celld has no account service, multi-tenant
  scheduler, or managed ingress.
- A fleet stores its durable state in an S3-compatible bucket, a Google Cloud
  Storage bucket, or an Azure Blob Storage container. The `celld dev` command
  instead uses a local SQLite object store. A regular node or an operator
  subcommand cannot select this local backend.
- A node does not rebalance the existing cells when it joins a fleet. Traffic
  assigns an unowned or released cell to a node with capacity.

## Networking and security

- celld does not terminate TLS. Terminate public TLS at an ingress proxy, and
  put the internal listener on a private network or an encrypted overlay.
- Peer traffic crosses the internal network as plaintext HTTP. The fleet HMAC
  authenticates tunnel establishment and control requests, and it does not
  encrypt application data on the wire. The network layer must provide the
  confidentiality.
- The fleet bucket controls the fleet. Give its credentials access to one fleet
  only. See [Security](security.md).

## Object storage credentials

- celld supports different credential methods for each object storage provider.
  See [Configure object storage](README.md#configure-object-storage) for the
  available methods and their precedence.
- Azure identity support is limited to the public Azure cloud. A managed
  identity from Azure App Service or Azure Container Apps does not work. Use a
  workload identity or a storage account key on these platforms.

## WebSockets

- An outbound Durable Object WebSocket keeps its cell resident. The connection
  closes if the cell moves to another node, so the application must store the
  connection intent and reconnect.
- A node limits the cells and outbound WebSockets that can remain resident.

## Platforms and updates

- The installer supplies binaries for Linux x86-64, Linux ARM64, and Apple
  Silicon. Windows is not supported.

display.text:
# WebAssembly

A Worker bundle can import a `.wasm` file. The import gives the
compiled module, not the bytes. This is the same rule that Wrangler
applies, so a bundle that runs on Cloudflare runs on celld without a
change.

```js
import addModule from "./add.wasm";

const { exports } = new WebAssembly.Instance(addModule);

export default {
  fetch() {
    return new Response(String(exports.add(2, 3)));
  },
};
```

`celld deploy` finds each wasm import, uploads the file beside the
bundle, and marks the deployment with the `wasm-v1` feature. A node
that predates this feature refuses the deployment with a clear
message, so a mixed fleet fails at deploy time and not at request
time.

celld compiles each wasm module once for the whole process. Every
isolate after the first one reuses the compiled module, so a cell
activation does not pay the compilation again.

## Rust with workers-rs

[workers-rs](https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-rs) compiles a Rust
crate to a Worker. The tool `worker-build` produces a JavaScript shim
and a wasm file, and the shim is a normal entry point for
`celld deploy`.

1. Install the build tool: `cargo install worker-build`.
2. Build the crate: `worker-build --release`.
3. Point the config at the shim:

```jsonc
{
  "name": "my-app",
  "main": "./build/worker/shim.mjs",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-01-01",
}
```

4. Deploy: `celld deploy`.

The shim wraps its exports in a JavaScript Proxy, and celld resolves
entrypoint classes and Durable Object classes through that wrapper.
The runtime surface that the application can use is the surface in
[Cloudflare compatibility](cloudflare-compat.md); a workers-rs API
that maps to a missing runtime feature does not work.

## The Worker Loader

A dynamically loaded worker can also carry wasm. Pass the bytes in the
`modules` map; a `BufferSource` value becomes a compiled-module import
in the loaded worker.

```js
const worker = env.loader.load({
  mainModule: "main.js",
  modules: {
    "main.js": `import m from "./add.wasm"; ...`,
    "add.wasm": wasmBytes,
  },
});
```

## Limits

The wasm bytes count against the deployment size limits, exactly as
JavaScript modules do. A wasm module that does not compile fails the
importing module with a `WebAssembly.CompileError` that names the
file.

1: // Copyright 2026 Deno Land Inc. Apache-2.0 license.
2: 
3: //! The isolate pool, reified sans-IO.
4: //!
5: //! celld runs JS on a set of isolates that grow and shrink with demand. An
6: //! isolate is not bound to a thread: `v8::Locker` installs the entering
7: //! thread's per-isolate state, so any worker can take an isolate and run a
8: //! turn in it. What an isolate *is* bound to is the JS state it holds, and
9: //! that is what every decision here is about.
10: //!
11: //! Two quantities, because they answer different questions:
12: //!
13: //! - **turns** — turns in flight on this isolate: queued for it plus the
14: //!   one running. CPU demand. A request awaiting I/O contributes nothing,
15: //!   because the isolate is released across the await, so this is what
16: //!   placement balances. It must count the queue, not just the runner: an
17: //!   isolate serves one turn at a time, so "executing" never exceeds one
18: //!   and could never signal that another isolate would help.
19: //! - **requests** — requests affiliated with this isolate. A request runs
20: //!   its first turn somewhere and its promise then lives in that isolate's
21: //!   heap, so every later turn must come back. Affiliation is memory, not
22: //!   CPU, and is what admission and shedding care about.
23: //!
24: //! Everything here is a predicate over observed load. The shell reports what
25: //! it sees and performs what it is told; it never decides.
26: 
27: /// Which isolate. An index the shell keeps, stable for that isolate's life.
28: /// Never a thread id — an isolate has no thread.
29: pub type IsolateId = usize;
30: 
31: /// What the shell observes about one isolate.
32: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Default, PartialEq, Eq)]
33: pub struct IsolateLoad {
34:     /// Turns in flight: waiting for this isolate plus the one running in it.
35:     /// Released across an await, so this is CPU demand rather than total
36:     /// outstanding work. Counting only the runner would cap this at one,
37:     /// since an isolate serves one turn at a time.
38:     pub turns: usize,
39:     /// Requests whose JS state lives here, running or awaiting. Each one
40:     /// pins a promise and its closures in this isolate's heap.
41:     pub requests: usize,
42:     /// Cells hosted here: realms this isolate holds, one per cell.
43:     ///
44:     /// The third quantity, and unlike the other two it does not come back on
45:     /// its own. A request ends; a cell stays until it is evicted or handed
46:     /// to another node. So this measures what the isolate is *committed* to,
47:     /// and it is what cell placement balances.
48:     pub cells: usize,
49:     /// The shell has stopped affiliating new work and is draining this
50:     /// isolate.
51:     pub retiring: bool,
52: }
53: 
54: /// Pool-wide limits, built once from configuration by the caller. The core
55: /// never reads the environment itself.
56: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
57: pub struct PoolLimits {
58:     /// Turns in flight at which an isolate is considered busy, so the pool
59:     /// prefers to grow rather than queue another turn behind those. Small:
60:     /// a couple of turns already waiting means another isolate would help.
61:     pub grow_at: usize,
62:     /// Per-isolate turn level the pool must stay under for a retirement to be
63:     /// worth starting. Below `grow_at`, and the gap is the hysteresis that
64:     /// stops growth and retirement chasing each other.
65:     pub shrink_under: usize,
66:     /// Ceiling on live isolates. Past it the pool queues rather than grows.
67:     pub max_stateless: usize,
68:     /// Affiliated stateless requests the node may hold at once, across every
69:     /// isolate. `None` leaves admission unbounded, which is only correct
70:     /// while something else caps concurrency.
71:     ///
72:     /// A node-wide figure rather than a per-isolate one, because the memory
73:     /// it bounds is the node's: a suspended request pins its promise and
74:     /// buffers wherever it landed, and spreading the same requests over more
75:     /// isolates does not make them cheaper.
76:     pub max_requests: Option<usize>,
77:     /// Cells one isolate may host. Past it, cell placement builds another
78:     /// isolate rather than adding a realm.
79:     ///
80:     /// A per-isolate figure where `max_requests` is node-wide, and the
81:     /// difference is not an inconsistency. A suspended request costs the
82:     /// same wherever it landed, so spreading requests buys nothing and the
83:     /// node-wide total is the real bound. Cells are not like that: they
84:     /// share one V8 heap, and a heap that holds too many of them is a
85:     /// single OOM taking every cell in it down together. Spreading is the
86:     /// whole point, so the bound has to be per-isolate.
87:     pub max_cells: usize,
88: }
89: 
90: /// The pool as the shell sees it. Indexed by [`IsolateId`].
91: #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
92: pub struct PoolLoad {
93:     pub isolates: Vec<IsolateLoad>,
94:     pub limits: PoolLimits,
95: }
96: 
97: /// Why a request was refused. The shell maps this to a status; a refusal is
98: /// a 503, because the node is the thing that is unavailable, not the request
99: /// that is wrong.
100: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
101: pub enum Refusal {
102:     /// The node already holds all the stateless requests it may.
103:     NodeFull,
104:     /// The node is shedding: it is over a resource ceiling and recovering.
105:     NodePressured,
106: }
107: 
108: /// Where a new request runs its first turn.
109: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
110: pub enum Placement {
111:     Existing(IsolateId),
112:     /// Build an isolate and use that. Growth is a placement outcome rather
113:     /// than a separate command, because an isolate cannot be addressed
114:     /// before the shell has built it.
115:     Grow,
116: }
117: 
118: impl PoolLoad {
119:     fn live(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = (IsolateId, &IsolateLoad)> {
120:         self.isolates
121:             .iter()
122:             .enumerate()
123:             .filter(|(_, l)| !l.retiring)
124:     }
125: 
126:     fn live_count(&self) -> usize {
127:         self.live().count()
128:     }
129: }
130: 
131: /// Take a stateless request, or refuse it.
132: ///
133: /// Admission and placement are one decision — *may this run, and where* —
134: /// so they are one call against one snapshot. Split apart they were two
135: /// views of the same node that could disagree, and the shell could admit a
136: /// request and then fail to place it, or place one it had never admitted.
137: ///
138: /// Called after the connection is accepted, not before. A node that stops
139: /// accepting leaves connections in its kernel backlog, where they wait
140: /// without an answer until the client's own deadline — the failure this
141: /// bound exists to prevent, arriving one layer lower. Accepting and refusing
142: /// costs a syscall and gives the caller a 503 it can act on.
143: ///
144: /// **Pressure does not close stateless admission.** It used to, and that was
145: /// wrong twice over.
146: ///
147: /// Transient work gives memory back on its own, so a request cheap enough to
148: /// drain by itself is not the thing to refuse.
149: ///
150: /// And it wedged the node's clients. The stateless Worker entry is also the
151: /// ingress that routes a cell to whichever node owns it, so refusing it does
152: /// not move load off a latched node; it removes that node's ability to move
153: /// load anywhere. A latched node must keep answering and place its cells on a
154: /// spare.
155: ///
156: /// What pressure does instead is **stop the pool growing**: a node over its
157: /// memory ceiling may keep serving on the isolates it already has, but must
158: /// not build another. Growth is still allowed when there is nothing to place
159: /// onto, because an isolate the node cannot build is a request it cannot
160: /// answer at all.
161: ///
162: /// Stateless memory is bounded by `max_requests`, which is the figure that
163: /// actually measures it.
164: pub fn admit(load: &PoolLoad, shedding: bool) -> Result<Placement, Refusal> {
165:     if let Some(max) = load.limits.max_requests {
166:         let held: usize = load.isolates.iter().map(|l| l.requests).sum();
167:         if held >= max {
168:             return Err(if shedding {
169:                 // Reported ahead of fullness: a full node drains on its own,
170:                 // a pressured one does not, so pressure is the more
171:                 // actionable thing to tell the caller.
172:                 Refusal::NodePressured
173:             } else {
174:                 Refusal::NodeFull
175:             });
176:         }
177:     }
178:     Ok(if shedding {
179:         place_without_growing(load)
180:     } else {
181:         place(load)
182:     })
183: }
184: 
185: /// [`place`], except that it will not build an isolate while one exists to
186: /// use. The node is over a memory ceiling; another heap is the last thing it
187: /// needs.
188: fn place_without_growing(load: &PoolLoad) -> Placement {
189:     match load.live().min_by_key(|(_, l)| l.turns) {
190:         Some((id, _)) => Placement::Existing(id),
191:         None => Placement::Grow,
192:     }
193: }
194: 
195: /// Choose the isolate for a request's first turn.
196: ///
197: /// This is the only free choice a stateless request gets. Every later turn of
198: /// that request is addressed to the isolate chosen here, because its promise
199: /// lives in that heap — so the shell must remember the affiliation, and this
200: /// function is not consulted again for that request.
201: ///
202: /// Balanced on turns in flight rather than affiliations, because an awaiting
203: /// request occupies nothing: an isolate holding a thousand suspended
204: /// requests and running no JS is idle and should be given work. Affiliation
205: /// count is a memory signal and belongs to admission, not here.
206: ///
207: /// Retiring isolates are skipped: the point of retiring one is that it stops
208: /// taking new affiliations.
209: pub fn place(load: &PoolLoad) -> Placement {
210:     match load.live().min_by_key(|(_, l)| l.turns) {
211:         // No isolate, or every one of them is draining.
212:         None => Placement::Grow,
213:         Some((id, l)) => {
214:             if l.turns >= load.limits.grow_at && load.live_count() < load.limits.max_stateless {
215:                 Placement::Grow
216:             } else {
217:                 // At the ceiling the pool queues. Refusing work is
218:                 // admission's job: see `worker::may_admit`.
219:                 Placement::Existing(id)
220:             }
221:         }
222:     }
223: }
224: 
225: /// Where a cell's realm goes, for the whole life of that cell on this node.
226: ///
227: /// **Not the same decision as [`place`], and the difference is permanence.**
228: /// A stateless request picks an isolate for its first turn and is done: the
229: /// next request picks again, so a bad choice costs one request. A cell's
230: /// realm holds its JS state, so every event it ever receives comes back
231: /// here. The shell records the assignment and never asks again — this is
232: /// consulted once per cell, not once per event.
233: ///
234: /// That makes the balance different too. `place` balances `turns`, because
235: /// an awaiting request occupies nothing and CPU is what a new turn contends
236: /// for. Here the cost is a realm that stays, so this reads `cells` and leaves
237: /// turns alone: an isolate running hot right now may still be the right home
238: /// for a cell that will outlive the burst.
239: ///
240: /// Growth happens at `max_cells` rather than at a busy-ness threshold, and
241: /// the ceiling is per-isolate for the reason in [`PoolLimits::max_cells`] —
242: /// too many cells in one heap is one OOM that takes all of them.
243: ///
244: /// There is no separate cell-isolate ceiling. The node-wide resident and RSS
245: /// limits decide whether this node can host another cell. Once ownership has
246: /// admitted the cell, placement always provides enough isolates to preserve
247: /// the per-isolate limit.
248: pub fn place_cell(load: &PoolLoad) -> Placement {
249:     // The fullest isolate that still has room, not the emptiest.
250:     //
251:     // Packing is what makes a heap reclaimable. The walk down evicts from the
252:     // isolate closest to empty, because only the cut that takes an isolate's
253:     // last cell returns its heap. Spreading aimed new cells at that same
254:     // isolate, so under any load that keeps admitting, eviction drained a heap
255:     // and placement refilled it: the isolate never reached zero, `retire`
256:     // refused it, and the node paid an eviction and a cold start per cell for
257:     // no memory back.
258:     //
259:     // Packing costs nothing that `max_cells` was not already bounding. That
260:     // ceiling is what limits how many cells one OOM can take, and it applies
261:     // either way.
262:     match load
263:         .live()
264:         .filter(|(_, l)| l.cells < load.limits.max_cells)
265:         .max_by_key(|(id, l)| (l.cells, std::cmp::Reverse(*id)))
266:     {
267:         // No isolate, or every one of them is draining.
268:         None => Placement::Grow,
269:         Some((id, _)) => Placement::Existing(id),
270:     }
271: }
272: 
273: /// Which isolate to retire, if any.
274: ///
275: /// Worth starting only when the rest of the pool can absorb the current turns
276: /// without immediately wanting to grow again.
277: ///
278: /// The victim is cheapest to empty: fewer affiliated requests, then the
279: /// newest, so a pool that grew for a burst gives back what the burst added.
280: /// An isolate empties itself as its requests finish, so the shell only has
281: /// to stop sending it work and wait.
282: ///
283: /// This returns a candidate, not a command. The shell still stops affiliating
284: /// new work and lets outstanding requests finish before the isolate goes
285: /// away — `Pool::reap`.
286: ///
287: /// **An isolate hosting a cell is never a candidate.** Retiring rests on the
288: /// victim emptying itself, and requests do that because they answer. A cell
289: /// does not: it stays until it is evicted or handed to another node, neither
290: /// of which retirement can cause. Choosing one would mark it retiring
291: /// forever — refused new work, never drained, never freed — which is a
292: /// smaller pool and a leak at the same time.
293: ///
294: /// Cell and stateless pools both run this maintenance decision. The cell pool
295: /// uses this filter to reclaim empty heaps after eviction while preserving
296: /// every isolate that still holds a realm.
297: /// May a RETIRING isolate's worker and heap be freed? Only when it is
298: /// provably drained: no queued or running turn, and no live affiliation.
299: /// An affiliation is any dispatched event's claim on the isolate, held
300: /// across suspensions — a suspended event holds no turn, so `turns`
301: /// alone is not drained-ness, and freeing on it re-enters a freed heap
302: /// when the event's host I/O completes (denoland/celld#147). `cells` is
303: /// consulted too: `retire` never selects a housed isolate, but a
304: /// generation-wide retirement marks every isolate of a superseded
305: /// deployment, housed or not, and freeing a housed one would drop every
306: /// resident cell in it. A cell whose residency dropped mid-event is still
307: /// the affiliation's case, not this one.
308: pub fn may_free(load: &IsolateLoad) -> bool {
309:     load.retiring && load.turns == 0 && load.requests == 0 && load.cells == 0
310: }
311: 
312: pub fn retire(load: &PoolLoad) -> Option<IsolateId> {
313:     let live = load.live().count();
314:     if live == 0 {
315:         return None;
316:     }
317: 
318:     let turns: usize = load.live().map(|(_, l)| l.turns).sum();
319:     let remaining = live - 1;
320:     if turns > remaining.saturating_mul(load.limits.shrink_under) {
321:         return None;
322:     }
323: 
324:     load.live()
325:         .filter(|(_, l)| l.cells == 0)
326:         .min_by_key(|(id, l)| (l.requests, std::cmp::Reverse(*id)))
327:         .map(|(id, _)| id)
328: }

(End of file - total 328 lines)

1: //! Cell-scope predicates, reified sans-IO.
2: //!
3: //! A cell scope names one Durable Object: `Class:instance`, or a bare instance
4: //! that the runtime prefixes with the single configured class. The scope is
5: //! then used as a path component and as an object-store key — `db_path` joins
6: //! it under the data directory, and the replication client builds
7: //! `cells/<scope>/ltx/e<epoch>` from it — so its charset is a SECURITY fence,
8: //! exactly as `peer::valid_identity`'s is. Admit `/` and a scope carries its
9: //! own path segments: it escapes the data directory through `..` and escapes
10: //! the bucket prefix the same way.
11: //!
12: //! The gate lives here, and the callers that accept a scope from the network
13: //! apply it before the scope reaches storage.
14: 
15: /// The fleet-wide storage limit for one cell scope. Every data filesystem must
16: /// support a path component of this size, so scope validity is the same on
17: /// every node that can own the cell.
18: pub const MAX_CELL_SCOPE: usize = 255;
19: 
20: /// Is a cell scope well-formed? Non-empty, at most `MAX_CELL_SCOPE` bytes, not
21: /// `.` or `..`, and only ASCII alphanumerics plus `_ - . : $`.
22: ///
23: /// The charset is the fence. `/` and `\` are excluded so the scope can never be
24: /// more than one path component, which is what makes an embedded `..` inert:
25: /// `Class:..` is a literal directory name, while `Class:../..` would traverse.
26: /// Control bytes and NUL are excluded with everything else outside the set.
27: ///
28: /// One path component is not sufficient on its own, because `.` and `..` are
29: /// themselves single components that the filesystem resolves. A bare `..`
30: /// clears the charset, and the callers that take a scope without a class prefix
31: /// — `/cell/`, `/evict/`, the peer routes, and the wake index — hand it to
32: /// `db_path` unchanged, so `data_dir.join("..")` lands above the data
33: /// directory. Both names are therefore rejected.
34: ///
35: /// `:` is admitted because it is the class/instance separator and an instance
36: /// may itself contain one. `$` is admitted because it is a legal JavaScript
37: /// identifier character, so it is a legal exported class name. Both are inert
38: /// in a path component.
39: ///
40: /// The bound is also the minimum `NAME_MAX` that celld accepts for a data
